name: VLOOKUP
description: VLOOKUP (Vertical Lookup) is a built-in function in Excel and Google Sheets that searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns a value in the same row from a specified column.
tldr: VLOOKUP searches for a value in the first column of a table array and returns a matching value from another column in the same row.

parameters.name: lookup_value
parameters.description: The value to search for in the first column of the table.

parameters.name: table_array
parameters.description: The range of cells that contains the data. The first column must contain the lookup_value.

parameters.name: col_index_num
parameters.description: The column number in the table_array from which to return a value.

parameters.name: range_lookup
parameters.description: Optional. TRUE (approximate match) or FALSE (exact match). Default is TRUE.

scenarios.title: Employee Salary Lookup
scenarios.description: HR managers often need to quickly find an employee's salary based on their employee ID. VLOOKUP is perfect for this task.
scenarios.outcome: Returns the salary for the employee with ID in cell A2 from the employee database.

scenarios.title: Product Price Lookup
scenarios.description: Online stores need to display product prices based on SKU codes. VLOOKUP can retrieve prices from a product catalog.
scenarios.outcome: Returns the price for the product with SKU in cell B2.

scenarios.title: Grade Lookup from Scores
scenarios.description: Teachers need to assign letter grades based on numeric scores. Using approximate match, VLOOKUP can find the appropriate grade.
scenarios.outcome: Returns the letter grade for the score in cell C2 based on a grading scale.

tutorialSteps.title: Prepare your data
tutorialSteps.description: Organize your data in a table format with the lookup values in the first column. Make sure the first column is sorted if using approximate match.

tutorialSteps.title: Enter the VLOOKUP formula
tutorialSteps.description: Click on the cell where you want the result to appear and type =VLOOKUP(
tutorialSteps.tip: Always start formulas with an equals sign (=)

tutorialSteps.title: Enter the lookup value
tutorialSteps.description: Select the cell containing the value you want to search for. This is the employee ID in our example.
tutorialSteps.tip: Make sure this value exists in the first column of your table array.

tutorialSteps.title: Select the table array
tutorialSteps.description: Highlight the entire table range including all columns you want to search through. Use absolute references ($) to lock the range.
tutorialSteps.tip: Press F4 after selecting the range to add dollar signs for absolute referencing.

tutorialSteps.title: Specify the column index
tutorialSteps.description: Enter the number of the column from which to return a value. Column 1 is the first column of the table.
tutorialSteps.tip: In our example, Department is in the 3rd column of the table array.

tutorialSteps.title: Choose match type and press Enter
tutorialSteps.description: Enter FALSE for exact match (most common) or TRUE for approximate match, then press Enter.

basicExample.description: Look up an employee's department based on their ID
basicExample.explanation: This formula searches for the value in cell A2 (employee ID) in the first column of the table $D$2:$F$10. When found, it returns the value from the 2nd column (Department).

advancedExamples.title: VLOOKUP with Wildcard
advancedExamples.description: Search for products using partial names with wildcard characters.
advancedExamples.explanation: The asterisk (*) wildcard matches any sequence of characters. This formula finds products that contain the text in cell A2 anywhere in their name.

advancedExamples.title: VLOOKUP with IFERROR
advancedExamples.description: Handle cases where the lookup value is not found to avoid #N/A errors.
advancedExamples.explanation: IFERROR wraps the VLOOKUP function and returns 'Not Found' instead of #N/A when the lookup value is not found in the table.

advancedExamples.title: Approximate Match for Grades
advancedExamples.description: Use approximate match to find letter grades based on numeric scores.
advancedExamples.explanation: With TRUE as the last argument, VLOOKUP finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value. The first column must be sorted in ascending order.

googleSheetsDeepDive.content:
VLOOKUP works identically in Google Sheets with the same syntax. However, Google Sheets offers several advantages and alternatives that make it more powerful for modern spreadsheet workflows.

One key difference is that Google Sheets supports ARRAYFORMULA with VLOOKUP, allowing you to apply the function to an entire column with a single formula. Google Sheets also has INDEX/MATCH as a more flexible alternative that supports left lookups.

examples.title: ARRAYFORMULA with VLOOKUP
examples.explanation: This formula applies VLOOKUP to the entire column A at once, returning results for each row automatically.

examples.title: VLOOKUP with IMPORTRANGE
examples.explanation: Combine VLOOKUP with IMPORTRANGE to search across different Google Sheets files.

howItWorks: VLOOKUP works by searching for the lookup_value in the first column of the table_array. When a match is found, it returns the value from the row where the match was found, from the column specified by col_index_num. With range_lookup set to FALSE (exact match), it finds an exact match or returns #N/A. With range_lookup set to TRUE (approximate match), it finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup_value, but requires the first column to be sorted.

howToSteps.name: Select a cell
howToSteps.text: Choose where you want the result to appear.

limitations: VLOOKUP can only search to the RIGHT of the lookup column. It cannot return values from columns to the left of the lookup column.
The column index number breaks when columns are inserted or deleted from the table_array.
Approximate match requires the first column to be sorted in ascending order.
VLOOKUP is not case-sensitive - it treats 'Apple' and 'apple' as the same value.

commonErrors.cause: The lookup value was not found in the first column
commonErrors.fix: Check if the lookup value exists in the first column of your table. Make sure there are no extra spaces. Use IFERROR to handle missing values gracefully.

commonErrors.cause: col_index_num is greater than the number of columns in table_array
commonErrors.fix: Make sure the column index number does not exceed the number of columns in your table array.

commonErrors.cause: col_index_num is less than 1 or range_lookup is not TRUE/FALSE
commonErrors.fix: Ensure col_index_num is at least 1 and range_lookup is either TRUE, FALSE, or omitted.

faq.question: Can VLOOKUP search to the left?
faq.answer: No, VLOOKUP can only search to the right. For left lookups, use INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP instead.

faq.question: What's the difference between TRUE and FALSE in VLOOKUP?
faq.answer: FALSE performs an exact match, while TRUE performs an approximate match (finds the closest value less than or equal to the lookup value).

faq.question: How do I make VLOOKUP case-sensitive?
faq.answer: VLOOKUP is not case-sensitive by default. To make it case-sensitive, use EXACT within INDEX/MATCH: =INDEX(B:B, MATCH(TRUE, EXACT(A:A, lookup_value), 0))
